issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 42-year-old project manager who came to treatment more than a year after a life-threatening medical crisis that began with what she had thought was an ordinary winter infection and escalated rapidly into an ICU admission. She remembers the fluorescent glare, the repeated attempts to place lines in her arms, the sting of needles, the plastic smell of antiseptic and saline, and the sharp cold she felt in the hospital as blankets slipped and staff moved quickly around her. Some parts remain fixed with unnatural precision-the glint of a drip stand, a nurse saying her oxygen was dropping-while whole stretches have vanished. What disturbs her is that the experience does not feel like a normal memory. It is so extreme that she sometimes says it seems as if it happened to "some other woman," yet at other times she is flooded by the same terror in her body with no image at all to explain it. After nights when those disjointed fragments pressed closer, she would move through the next day finding traces of the ICU everywhere, as if the memory itself had taught her to spot it in the fluorescent light of a conference room, the plastic packaging in the supply closet, or the bite of cold air in the garage.

In the months after she was discharged, those fragments began to intrude into ordinary life in ways that felt both sudden and incomprehensible. Walking past the first-aid cabinet at work and seeing packaged medical supplies could make her stomach drop before she even knew why. In her office building, the sharp disinfectant smell used by the cleaning crew was especially potent; on cold mornings, stepping out of the garage into winter air could bring on the same internal jolt. In those moments the thought came with alarming certainty that this was what her life had become-that her body had never really come back from the ICU and that a normal workday could still expose how permanently damaged she was. These moments did not just remind her of the hospitalization; they seemed to pull up disconnected shards of it, or else the raw emotional intensity without a picture, leaving her shaken by something she could not fully place. Because the reactions felt so immediate and bodily, Linh had come to believe they proved that her body had been permanently damaged and that her life had been ruined by what happened.

That meaning settled heavily into how she saw herself. Before the illness, she took pride in being the person who kept both her team and her household running, managing deadlines, meals, school forms, and family plans with brisk competence. Since the hospitalization, she has come to believe she failed in that most important role. When she feels herself go blank around the memory, or when only isolated moments return with unbearable force, she reads that fractured quality as evidence of how badly she was broken by the event. The unrealness of the story makes it no less devastating; if anything, she is frightened by what it means that something could happen to her body and mind so completely that it no longer feels like her own life.

These beliefs shape what she does with the memory. Linh tries hard to erase it whenever it starts to come near, shutting down any train of thought that might lead back to the hospital. Each time she had to steer so forcefully away from it, or catch herself checking whether she was still thinking clearly, it seemed to confirm her worst conclusion: that she was too fragile to bear what had happened and had been changed in some lasting way by it. At the same time, she monitors her own mind constantly, scanning for any sign that she is "losing it" because she worries that the moments of emotional flooding without clear images mean she is going crazy. The more she pushes the memory away and checks herself for signs of mental collapse, the less coherent it seems to become: only a few scenes remain painfully vivid, while the rest stay blank and unbelievable. That in turn strengthens her sense that something in her has been permanently harmed.

Her avoidance has spread into the structure of her days. As a project manager, she now asks colleagues to handle onsite visits when projects involve hospital clients, and she will reroute her commute if she knows it passes an emergency department entrance. She has postponed routine physical exams and leaves the room if a television show features an ambulance or an IV pole. For a moment these maneuvers feel protective, but they have made the triggers feel less predictable and more dangerous. A random antiseptic smell in the office restroom or a cold blast from the conference room vent can catch her off guard and set off the same wave of dread, and because she has had so little contact with medical settings, a glimpse of a needle or drip bag now feels almost unbearable.

By the time she sought help, the cycle had tightened around both work and family life. Her husband had become the one scheduling appointments she then canceled, and at work her careful avoidance was becoming visible enough that she worried colleagues were questioning her reliability. What finally brought her in was a recent incident during a winter meeting when the room was over-air-conditioned and a coworker opened a first-aid kit for a minor cut. Linh felt the full panic of the ICU in her body, with only a flash of tubing and then nothing she could organize into a story. She sat through the meeting silently checking whether she was still thinking clearly, terrified that this was proof she would never be herself again. What she wants most is to stop living as if one smell, one cold room, or one glimpse of medical equipment can take her out of her own life, though she is deeply afraid that the damage has already been done.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers lead to or strengthen Linh’s negative appraisals about being permanently damaged or ruined.
The vignette does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that Linh’s trauma memory itself increases or generates triggers/reminders.
The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Linh’s avoidance or checking directly intensifies her negative appraisals, rather than the memory changes doing so.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers lead to or strengthen Linh’s negative appraisals about being permanently damaged or ruined.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly convey in one paragraph that Linh’s trauma memory itself increases or generates triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Linh’s avoidance or checking directly intensifies her negative appraisals, rather than the memory changes doing so.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
